analysis.one_liner: Makes small-dollar lenders register with regulators and blocks them from draining borrowers' bank accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee on September 19, 2024, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single additional cosponsor as the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets online payday-style lending. It would require lenders of loans under $5,000 and under a year to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, require those loans to follow the interest-rate and fee laws of the borrower's own state, ban overdraft fees on prepaid card accounts, stop lenders from pulling money from a borrower's bank account without written permission, and ban companies from selling borrowers' bank account numbers and Social Security numbers to loan lead brokers unless they are actually making the loan. It also orders a government study of small-dollar lending on tribal reservations.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use payday, installment, and other small-dollar loans, especially online borrowers. They would get protections when lenders reach into their bank accounts, limits on junk fees, and the guarantee that the rate caps and fee limits of their home state apply to a loan made over the internet.

how_it_helps.text: A remotely created check (a payment order that can drain a bank account without a real signature) could only be issued by a person the consumer specifically authorized in writing, and the consumer could revoke that authorization at any time [S2].

Loans under $5,000 repaid in under a year would be treated as preauthorized transfers under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, giving borrowers the legal right to stop payments that today are hard to reverse [S2].

Small-dollar lenders and the companies that broker or arrange their applications would have to register with the CFPB before issuing credit, and internet, phone, mail, and national-bank small-dollar loans would have to comply with the annual percentage rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives [S2].
Overdraft fees on prepaid card accounts would be banned, so a transaction over the balance could be declined but never charged [S2].

Companies could not broker or distribute sensitive personal financial information (Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers) for a small-dollar loan unless they were directly making the loan, cutting off lead-generation websites that pass bank data to a network of lenders [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online payday and installment lenders, lead-generation websites that sell borrowers' bank data, prepaid card issuers that charge overdraft fees, and national banks that use online small-dollar lending to charge rates a borrower's home state would not allow. Consumers with poor credit could also see fewer loan options if state rate caps make some loans unprofitable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online payday lenders and data brokers

drawbacks.text: Small-dollar lenders often argue that state rate caps and compliance costs make it unprofitable to serve borrowers with poor credit, so some of those borrowers could lose access to any credit and fall back on worse options; the bill itself acknowledges access concerns by requiring a GAO study of the availability of capital on tribal reservations [S2].

The bill hands broad rulemaking discretion to the CFPB, including the power to define which transactions count as small-dollar credit and to bar additional prepaid fees, which lenders and their allies criticized as an expansion of unelected regulatory power [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers trapped in repeat cycles of high-rate small-dollar debt, the protections — control over bank account withdrawals, state rate caps applied to internet loans, an end to prepaid overdraft fees, and a ban on data-hungry lead brokers — outweigh the cost of less access to marginal loans. The genuine trade-off is that stricter rules can shrink the supply of credit for the riskiest borrowers, which the bill partially acknowledges with its tribal-availability study rather than resolving.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on September 19, 2024, with Representatives Jayapal, Garcia of Texas, and Porter as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which was its last recorded action; no hearing, markup, or vote followed [S4].

The bill ended the Congress with only its four original Democratic cosponsors and no Senate companion, and the Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025, killing it under the rule that bills die when a Congress ends [S1][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online small-dollar lenders, lead-generation websites, and prepaid overdraft-fee collectors are better off, because the registration requirement, state rate-cap mandate, and data restrictions they faced never advanced. Borrowers are no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Reps. Jayapal, Garcia of Texas, and Porter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no additional members joined before it died.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 19, 2024 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the bill never left the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee and had no Republican support on record.

industries.note: These lenders would have to register with the CFPB before making loans under $5,000, and internet and national-bank small-dollar loans would have to obey the borrower's home-state rate and fee caps, directly cutting the rates and fees that make repeat high-cost borrowing profitable [S2]. Borrowers would gain real payment protections instead of paying inflated rates.

The bill bans these companies from distributing borrowers' Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers for small-dollar loans unless they directly make the loan, ending the business model that funnels one application to many lenders and drives repeat borrowing [S2].

industries.industry: Prepaid card issuers and payment processors
industries.note: Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts would be banned, eliminating a fee stream charged disproportionately to consumers who use prepaid cards because they lack bank accounts [S2].

industries.industry: National banks making online small-dollar loans
industries.note: The state-law compliance requirement would end these banks' ability to charge rates online that a borrower's home state prohibits, a revenue loss, though it does not touch their core banking business [S2].
